extracted.intended_audience: writers, journalists, literary critics, and biographers interested in standards for newspaper writing and ethical biography practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles about writing for daily newspapers and the ethics of publishing private/biographical material, drawn from a literary-biographical discussion of Coleridge's journalism and posthumous representation. Covers what kinds of writing succeed in journals, obligations of independence and trust, timeliness, and limits on publishing private documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation insufficient for daily newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: "The reputation of the writings of any man, the mere reputation of them, would not serve, or in the very slightest degree serve, any daily newspaper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and publishers value immediate news-worthiness and fit-for-purpose material over an author's general literary reputation. A celebrated literary reputation alone will not guarantee placement or usefulness in a daily paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: High and careful writing is impractical for daily journals
rubrics_metrics.description: "High and careful writing for the daily journal will never answer: who could furnish noble views and a refined moral commentary on public events and occurrences every day of the week, or even every other day...?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daily journalism demands timeliness and regular output; sustained, elaborate moral or philosophical essays are impractical on a day-to-day schedule. Expect editors to prefer shorter, more immediate pieces over long, finely wrought commentary for routine publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors prefer news and short leading paragraphs to brilliant writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Street always preferring news, and a short notice of it in a leading paragraph, to any writing, however brilliant,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical editorial priorities favor concise reporting and brief lead notices; even very high-quality, 'brilliant' prose may be rejected if it doesn't suit the immediate news needs or space constraints of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse or low writing on important subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: "On the other hand, a coarse or low sort of writing on the important subjects, with which the journal deals, must do mischief."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing weighty public matters, maintain quality and avoid vulgar or low treatment; poor-quality treatment of significant subjects can damage public discourse and the paper's influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and regularity are essential for press work
rubrics_metrics.description: "He never could write a thing that was immediately required of him."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working for the press requires the ability to produce material on demand and on schedule. Failure to provide timely copy reduces the chance of insertion and diminishes a writer's utility to a daily paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact judged by intensity as well as quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Men are apt to judge of their labors by intensity as much as by quantity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate journalistic or essayistic contributions not only by how many pieces were produced but by the intensity and memorable effect of individual pieces; a few powerful essays may outweigh many routine items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine impartiality plus literary talent secures success
rubrics_metrics.description: "Genuine impartiality with a respectable portion of literary talent will secure the success of a newspaper without ministerial patronage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A newspaper's credibility and circulation grow from a believable claim to impartiality combined with competent literary quality—independence and talent can substitute for political patronage in winning readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain both independence and the appearance of independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should "maintain and assert not only its independence, but its appearance of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception matters: even if a paper pursues practical alliances, it must preserve both genuine editorial independence and the public appearance of independence to retain influence and respect; sliding visibly toward becoming an organ of government undermines trust and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in the person and paper is necessary for influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The text emphasizes "the faith in the person and paper which brings them forward."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers' belief in the integrity of the author and publication underpins persuasive impact; losing that faith leads audiences to ascribe writings to partisan motives rather than to conviction or merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colloquial style and evident good sense assist political journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Morning Post's influence was aided by "a colloquial style and evident good sense, in which, as acting on an immense mass of knowledge of existing men and existing circumstances, you are superior to any man I ever met with in my life-time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For political and persuasive journalism, an accessible conversational tone combined with sound judgment and demonstrated knowledge of people and affairs enhances reach and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish private/secret histories of living persons for public good alone
rubrics_metrics.description: "I should never think the public good a sufficient apology for publishing the secret history of any man or woman whatever, who had connexions remaining upon earth;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographers and publishers should subordinate claimed public benefit to the prior claims of private and natural interests (family, surviving relations). Revealing intimate private material about living relations requires special moral justification and, generally, restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give private notices or documents to nearest relatives rather than publish them yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a finished portrait of one, in whom they are nearly concerned, is due to the world, they alone can be the debtors, for the property by inheritance is in them. Other persons, without their leave, should not undertake to give any such portrait;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in possession of private letters or intimate documents, the responsible course is to place them in the hands of the subject's nearest relatives and let them decide on publication, rather than unilaterally publishing sensitive material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate potential public advantage to private/natural interests regarding disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: "All such considerations of advantage to the public should be subordinated to the prior claims of private and natural interests."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if publishing private facts might lead to medical or social benefits, the obligation to protect private persons and their families typically takes precedence; editors and biographers should favor privacy when lives and relations are affected.
